question: How do I know if a lump on my dog is a lipoma or something dangerous?
answer: You don't — not by looking or feeling it, and that's the whole point. Mast cell tumours are called the great imitators because they can look and feel identical to a harmless fatty lump, a skin tag, or even a nipple. The only way to know is cells under a microscope. For a lump on the surface your vet can do an impression smear (press a slide against it, no needle). For a lump buried under the skin you need a fine needle aspirate, which draws cells from the CENTRE of the mass. Anyone telling you a lump is 'just a fatty tumour' without having looked at cells is guessing. (Clinical/holistic veterinary practice guidance; the imitator problem is also documented in the conventional literature.)
source: Holistic veterinary practice guidance (Kyle Cabral research compilation, 2026-08-20)

question: When should I worry about a lump on my dog?
answer: Book a vet visit if: the lump is brand new; an old lump suddenly changes size, shape or texture; it has irregular borders; it is growing fast; or your dog keeps licking and obsessing over it. The reassuring flip side — a lump that has not changed at all in five years is very likely nothing. The habit that catches problems early is running your hands over your dog's ENTIRE body every day, including legs, belly and mammary glands, not just the obvious spots. You are feeling for something new, or something old that has changed. (Clinical practice guidance.)

question: Does a benign lipoma need to be surgically removed?
answer: Usually no — true lipomas are benign and most are left alone. Two situations change that. First, when one grows large enough to interfere with movement, especially in the armpit or the groin. Second, when it gets big enough to outgrow its own blood supply: the core tissue dies, liquefies, and drains a thick pus-like fluid. That fluid is dead tissue, not an infection. The practical advice from vets who do these removals: if it is coming out, take it while it is still a manageable size. Removing a grapefruit-to-watermelon-sized mass leaves a huge empty pocket under the skin that then has to heal. (Clinical surgical experience.)
source: Holistic veterinary practice guidance (Kyle Cabral research compilation, 2026-08-20)

question: Why does my dog's lipoma have fluid draining out of it?
answer: This happens with very large lipomas. The mass grows past what its own blood supply can feed, so the tissue at the centre dies and liquefies, then drains out through the skin as a thick pus-like discharge. It looks like an abscess but it is dead fat tissue, not infection. It is a sign the lipoma has gotten too big and should be assessed for removal. See your vet — this is not something to manage at home. (Clinical observation.)
source: Holistic veterinary practice guidance (Kyle Cabral research compilation, 2026-08-20)

question: What causes lipomas in dogs according to holistic vets?
answer: In Traditional Chinese Veterinary Medicine a lipoma is a pocket of abnormal phlegm that the body creates to wall off toxins it cannot clear. The framing is that this is driven by liver congestion — the liver is overloaded, so the body stores the overflow. The tell that supports this reading clinically is WHERE they appear: lipomas cluster along the gallbladder meridian, meaning armpits, flanks, and the inside of the back legs. This is a TCVM model and a clinical observation, not a mechanism that has been demonstrated in a controlled canine study. It is useful because it points at a specific set of interventions — reduce toxin load, clear dampness — that practitioners report working.
source: TCVM framework / holistic veterinary practice (Kyle Cabral research compilation, 2026-08-20)

question: Which foods should I avoid if my dog gets lipomas?
answer: The TCVM 'damp-building' list, which practitioners tell lipoma-prone dogs to cut: pork, fatty meats including lamb and duck, green-lipped mussel, eggs, honey, spirulina, slippery elm, and marshmallow root. Note that several of these — green-lipped mussel and eggs especially — are excellent foods in other contexts, so this is specifically about a dog that is forming fatty lumps, not a general 'bad food' list. The bigger lever than any single ingredient is getting off dry kibble entirely and onto fresh, raw, or gently cooked food. (TCVM dietary framework, clinical practice.)
source: TCVM framework / holistic veterinary practice (Kyle Cabral research compilation, 2026-08-20)

question: What foods help dry out dampness for a dog with lipomas?
answer: The drying foods used in TCVM for lipoma-prone dogs: celery, alfalfa, chamomile, turmeric, parsley, pumpkin, ginger, kelp, seaweed, and baked sweet potato. One specific detail that matters — the sweet potato must be BAKED or ROASTED, not boiled. Baking is said to concentrate its drying properties; boiling does the opposite and adds moisture. (TCVM dietary framework, clinical practice, no trial evidence.)
source: TCVM framework / holistic veterinary practice (Kyle Cabral research compilation, 2026-08-20)

question: Should I feed my dog cold food from the fridge?
answer: No — and this matters more than most owners realise if you are managing lipomas or dampness. In TCVM, cold food straight from the refrigerator damages digestive energy and builds dampness, which is the exact thing you are trying to clear. Warm it slightly or leave it out until it reaches room temperature before serving. This applies to raw, gently cooked, and any refrigerated fresh food. (TCVM principle, clinical practice.)
source: TCVM framework / holistic veterinary practice (Kyle Cabral research compilation, 2026-08-20)

question: Can medications cause lipomas in dogs?
answer: Holistic practitioners report that certain drugs are hard on the liver and frequently precede multiple lipomas appearing: levothyroxine (thyroid medication), gabapentin, and NSAIDs. Over-vaccinating is named alongside these. This is a pattern reported from practice, not a demonstrated causal link — and importantly, none of these are drugs to stop on your own. If your dog is on long-term medication and developing multiple lumps, that is a conversation to have with your vet about liver support and whether the dose or drug still fits, not a reason to discontinue treatment.
source: Holistic veterinary clinical observation (Kyle Cabral research compilation, 2026-08-20)

question: My dog has multiple lipomas — should I test for tick-borne disease?
answer: Yes, ask your vet about it. Chronic tick-borne infection like Lyme disease congests the liver and immune system, and holistic practitioners link that congestion to widespread lipoma formation. The specific test to request is a C6 antibody test. This is worth doing specifically when a dog has MULTIPLE bumps rather than one isolated lump — multiple masses point at a systemic driver rather than a local one. (Clinical observation; the liver-congestion mechanism is a TCVM framing, but the C6 test itself is a standard validated diagnostic.)
source: Holistic veterinary clinical observation (Kyle Cabral research compilation, 2026-08-20)

question: What is the L-carnitine dose for dog lipomas?
answer: 50 mg per kilogram of body weight, twice daily. The reasoning is that L-carnitine targets fat metabolism and actively breaks down fat cells, and it also supports muscle mass. L-carnitine itself is well tolerated in dogs and is commonly used for heart conditions, so the safety profile is established even though the lipoma use is not. Be straight with yourself about the evidence tier: this dose comes from holistic veterinary practice, and there is no controlled canine trial testing L-carnitine against a lipoma.
source: Holistic veterinary protocol (Kyle Cabral research compilation, 2026-08-20)

question: How much green tea extract can I give my dog for lipomas?
answer: 50 mg per 10 lbs of body weight daily, sprinkled on food. For a 20 lb dog that works out to roughly a quarter of a standard 400 mg capsule. The key detail is that it must be a concentrated EXTRACT — brewed green tea does not deliver the same dose and practitioners report it does not produce the same result. The proposed mechanism is raising metabolic rate and fat oxidation to target fat cells. (Holistic veterinary protocol; no canine lipoma trial exists.)
source: Holistic veterinary protocol (Kyle Cabral research compilation, 2026-08-20)

question: What is the colostrum dose for dogs with lipomas?
answer: 100 mg per 10 lbs of body weight daily. The rationale is that colostrum increases metabolic rate and promotes muscle mass, which shifts body composition away from fat storage, and it supports the immune system at the same time. It is considered very safe and has a useful side benefit — it helps coat the intestinal tract, which is why it is also used to buffer the gut side effects of NSAIDs. (Holistic veterinary protocol; no canine lipoma trial.)
source: Holistic veterinary protocol (Kyle Cabral research compilation, 2026-08-20)

question: How do I dose MCT oil for a dog with lipomas?
answer: Start at half a teaspoon per 20 lbs of body weight daily and work up to 1 teaspoon per 20 lbs daily. Two timing rules matter. Start slowly or you will cause diarrhoea — MCT oil is notorious for it if you jump straight to the full dose. And give it at least 4 weeks before you judge whether it is doing anything; that is the assessment window practitioners use. The mechanism given is conversion to ketones, which raises metabolic rate and supports fat loss while preserving muscle. (Holistic veterinary protocol; no canine lipoma trial.)
source: Holistic veterinary protocol (Kyle Cabral research compilation, 2026-08-20)

question: How do you use DMSO and aloe vera on a dog's lipoma?
answer: A 70/30 mix of liquid DMSO and aloe vera applied directly onto the lipoma twice daily. The idea is that DMSO penetrates skin rapidly and carries the aloe into the mass, triggering a localised immune response that prompts the body to attack the fatty growth. A mild inflammatory reaction at the site is expected. CRITICAL SAFETY POINT: always wear gloves. DMSO's whole property is rapid skin penetration, which means it carries whatever is on the skin straight into the bloodstream — including whatever is on YOUR hands. This is a holistic protocol with no controlled canine trial behind it, and it should be run past your vet first.
source: Holistic veterinary protocol (Kyle Cabral research compilation, 2026-08-20)

question: What mushroom dose is used for dog lipomas?
answer: For a 20 lb dog: 0.5 g to 1 g of hot-water-extracted turkey tail powder, twice daily. Turkey tail and maitake are both used, and the stated mechanism is increasing Phase II liver detoxification so the body can process the walled-off toxins, plus anti-tumour properties. Two details practitioners emphasise: the product must be HOT WATER EXTRACTED — raw mushroom powder is not the same thing and will not perform the same way — and lipoma dosing sits below the higher doses (up to 3 g twice daily) used for cancer. (Holistic veterinary protocol; the liver detox mechanism is not established in canine lipoma specifically.)
source: Holistic veterinary protocol (Kyle Cabral research compilation, 2026-08-20)

question: How do I know if my dog is a 'warm' or 'cool' dog for choosing herbs?
answer: You read their behaviour. A WARM dog pants, seeks out cold floors and tile, and sprawls out to dump heat. A COOL dog seeks warmth, wants blankets, curls up tight, and lies in the sun. This matters because the lipoma herbs split by constitution and giving the wrong one works against you. For COOL dogs: calendula tincture for lymphatics, plus ashwagandha (especially if hypothyroid), turmeric, and self-heal (Prunella vulgaris). For WARM dogs: cleavers tincture for lymphatics, plus burdock root (helps process fats), chickweed, and violet. (TCVM constitutional framework, clinical practice.)
source: TCVM framework / holistic veterinary practice (Kyle Cabral research compilation, 2026-08-20)

question: How many drops of calendula or cleavers tincture do I give my dog?
answer: Twice daily, dosed by size, given directly in the mouth: a Chihuahua-sized dog gets 1 drop; a 20 lb dog (King Charles Spaniel size) gets 2 drops; a Corgi gets 3-4 drops; a Golden Retriever gets 4-5 drops; a giant breed gets 5-6 drops. Cleavers is for warm dogs and cools the core; calendula is for cool dogs and warms it. One practical warning on cleavers: it is a diuretic and may cause loose stool for the first 24 hours. (Holistic veterinary protocol.)
source: Holistic veterinary protocol (Kyle Cabral research compilation, 2026-08-20)

question: How fast should I add new herbs to my dog's lipoma protocol?
answer: One at a time, three days apart. This is not caution for its own sake — if you add three herbs at once and your dog gets digestive upset, you have no idea which one caused it and you have to unwind the whole protocol. Three days is enough to see a reaction. The same principle applies to MCT oil, which needs its own slow titration to avoid diarrhoea. (Standard holistic practice guidance.)
source: Holistic veterinary protocol (Kyle Cabral research compilation, 2026-08-20)

question: Do I need digestive enzymes when switching my dog off kibble?
answer: Holistic practitioners recommend them for 3 to 6 months after the transition from kibble to raw or fresh food. The reasoning in TCVM terms is boosting 'digestive fire' while the gut adapts, and practically it supports fat digestion and helps process the residue from years of inflammatory kibble. It is considered especially important for dogs with low stomach acid or a poor microbiome. After that window most dogs no longer need them. (Holistic veterinary practice; timeline is clinical convention, not trial-derived.)
source: Holistic veterinary protocol (Kyle Cabral research compilation, 2026-08-20)

question: When should I NOT try natural remedies on my dog's lump?
answer: Before you have cells looked at. This is the single most important rule in the whole topic. Every dissolving protocol here assumes you have CONFIRMED the mass is a benign lipoma by impression smear or fine needle aspirate. Treating an unconfirmed lump at home means that if it is actually a mast cell tumour or another malignancy, you have spent weeks or months letting it grow. Also skip the home protocol and go straight to your vet if the lump is growing rapidly, has irregular borders, is interfering with movement, or is draining fluid. Natural management is for confirmed benign lipomas in a stable dog — nothing else.
source: Holistic veterinary practice guidance (Kyle Cabral research compilation, 2026-08-20)

question: Can exercise help prevent lipomas in dogs?
answer: Practitioners say yes, and the reasoning is specific: the lymphatic system is what transports body fats, and unlike the circulatory system it has no pump — it moves when the body moves. Regular exercise plus lower back stimulation keeps lymph flowing and is said to prevent the fatty congestion that becomes a lipoma. This is a mechanistic and clinical argument rather than a trial finding, but it costs nothing and the general health case for exercise is independently solid. (Clinical observation.)
source: Holistic veterinary practice guidance (Kyle Cabral research compilation, 2026-08-20)
